definition: In autonomous vehicle testing, a perception error model (PEM) is an approach to simulating the behaviour of sensing and perception systems by modeling the errors they produce rather than simulating the underlying sensor physics.
details: This differs from high-fidelity sensor simulation techniques, where one wishes to generate synthetic sensor signals that the actual perception algorithms would process. Perception error models are sometimes referred to as surrogate models for perception systems, because they approximate the output of computationally expensive object detectors at a fraction of the computational cost. The primary motivation for PEMs is to enable efficient virtual testing of autonomous vehicle driving policies. Since the failure modes of perception systems have significant impact on downstream planning and control, testing these systems requires capturing the dependencies between perception errors and vehicle behaviour. PEMs provide a computationally efficient alternative to running full physics-based sensor simulations with actual perception algorithms.

explainer.lead: A perception error model simulates a perception system by reproducing the errors it makes rather than simulating the underlying sensor physics. It exists mainly to make virtual testing of autonomous vehicle driving policies computationally cheap.

tiers.eli5: Instead of recreating a whole camera and lens to test a self-driving car in a game, you just inject the kinds of mistakes the camera software tends to make.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use PEMs as surrogate models to approximate expensive object detectors at a fraction of the computational cost during policy testing. The pitfall is that the model captures error patterns, not sensor physics, so it differs from high-fidelity sensor simulation that generates synthetic signals for real perception algorithms.
tiers.paperLevel: A perception error model is an approach to simulating sensing and perception systems by modeling the errors they produce rather than simulating sensor physics; it acts as a surrogate for perception systems, approximating computationally expensive object detectors at lower cost.

explainer.example: A driving policy is tested in simulation where a PEM injects object-detection errors instead of rendering synthetic camera signals for a full detector to process.
